First Aid for Suspected Fractures
Immediate Care Before Medical Help Arrives
A fracture is a broken or cracked bone, most often caused by a fall, accident, sports injury, or direct blow. Fractures can range from a small hairline crack to a bone that has broken through the skin. Any suspected fracture needs professional medical evaluation. The goal of first aid is not to treat the fracture itself, but to keep the injured person safe, prevent further damage, and support them until trained medical help takes over.
What to Do Immediately
1. Stay calm and keep the injured person calm. Reassure them and encourage them to stay still, since anxiety and movement can make the injury worse.
2. Check for danger first. Make sure the surroundings are safe before approaching, and do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger (such as fire, traffic, or floodwater).
3. Keep the injured part still. Support the limb or area gently in the position you found it, using your hands, a rolled towel, or cushions to prevent movement.
4. Control any bleeding. If there is a wound, apply gentle, firm pressure around it (not directly on a protruding bone) using a clean cloth or sterile dressing.
5. Immobilize only if trained and help is delayed. A firm object such as a folded newspaper, magazine, or board can be placed alongside the limb and secured loosely with cloth strips, padded so it does not press directly on the skin.
6. Apply a cold pack if available. Wrap ice or a cold pack in a cloth (never place it directly on skin) and hold it near, not on, the injury site for short periods to reduce swelling and pain.
7. Watch for shock. If the person looks pale, feels faint, or is breathing rapidly, help them lie down, keep them warm, and if there is no suspected spinal, head, or leg injury, raise their legs slightly.
8. Monitor breathing and responsiveness continuously until emergency responders arrive, and be ready to describe what happened and what care has already been given.
What NOT to Do
• Do not try to straighten, realign, or push a bent limb or a bone back into place, even if it looks deformed.
• Do not push a bone that is sticking out of the skin back in, and do not touch or probe an open wound.
• Do not move the person unnecessarily, especially if a neck, back, hip, or thigh injury is suspected, as improper movement can cause serious additional harm.
• Do not let the injured person walk on or use the injured limb, even if they insist they can manage.
• Do not apply ice directly to bare skin, as this can cause cold burns.
• Do not give food, water, or medication by mouth, in case surgery or anesthesia is needed soon after.
• Do not attempt a splint if you are not trained and help is only minutes away; an incorrectly applied splint can restrict blood flow or worsen the injury.
• Do not ignore signs of numbness, tingling, or a cold, pale limb below the injury, as this suggests blood flow or nerve involvement that needs urgent attention.
When to Call Emergency Services
Call an ambulance (108 in India, or the local emergency number) immediately if any of the following apply:
• The bone has broken through the skin, or there is heavy or uncontrolled bleeding.
• A fracture of the skull, spine, neck, hip, pelvis, or thigh bone is suspected.
• The injured person is unconscious, unresponsive, or not breathing normally.
• There is visible deformity, or the limb appears at an unnatural angle.
• The person shows signs of shock: pale or clammy skin, rapid breathing, dizziness, or confusion.
• The area beyond the injury (fingers or toes) becomes numb, cold, or discolored.
• The injury resulted from a major fall, road accident, or high-impact trauma.
• You are unsure of the severity, since it is always safer to seek professional evaluation for a suspected fracture.
Source Basis
This guidance reflects general first-aid principles for fractures as commonly described by established public health and emergency medicine organizations, including recognized international and Indian emergency care bodies. It is a general awareness summary in original wording and is not a substitute for certified first-aid training or professional medical instructions.
